Hypothesis

I used Claude Sonnet 5 to brainstorm ideas for this section. The AI said I should not claim "people moved" or "ideas spread", do not write a null that just says "there is no pattern", do not make it vague, clustering is not sufficient evidence, and don't bundle all artifacts together as they might have independently spread. 

Hypothesis: The distribution of lithics (tanged points, Zinken, and geometric microliths) across Late Glacial Europe between space and time suggests a non-random, directional gradient. This pattern is consistent with the claim that tool assemblages were spread via migration rather than independent invention. 
Null Hypothesis: The spatial and temporal distribution of lithics (tanged points, Zinken, and geometric microliths) across Late Glacial Europe cannot be distinguished from random. This is consistent with the idea that tools were independently locally invented rather than spreading via migration between sites. 
Alternative explanation:This pattern may also be produced by sampling bias. For example, sites sampled more intensively might be overestimated while those that were not excavated as intensively might be underestimated.

The key variables I need to test my hypothesis are site, artifact type, and timeslice. Testing these threee variable will allow me to analyze the time and location of an artifact. The location where the oldest artifact of that type is found will tell me where it might have originated. The weakest link is region because site will tell us a more specific region anyways.
```{r}
## asked AI to create the code below:
library(tidyverse)

lithics <- read.csv("data/outlines_AR_fac_artefactnames_w_metric_measures.csv")

lithics_sub <- lithics %>%
  mutate(Trait = case_when(
    TaxUnit %in% c("Ahr", "Swid", "Brom") ~ "Tanged points",
    TaxUnit %in% c("Feder", "ABPFeder", "HFeder", "AFeder") ~ "Zinken",
    TaxUnit %in% c("Sauv", "ESauv", "Meso", "EMeso", "Magle") ~ "Geometric microliths",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  )) %>%
  drop_na(Trait, Long, Lat, Timeslice)

world_map <- map_data("world")

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = world_map, aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(data = lithics_sub, aes(x = Long, y = Lat, color = Timeslice),
             size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-10, 40), ylim = c(35, 60)) +
  facet_wrap(~ Trait) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(name = "Time Period") +
  labs(
    title = "Spatial-Temporal Distribution of Toolkit Traits Across Late Glacial Europe",
    subtitle = "Faceted by trait type, coloured by time period",
    x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()


```

```{r}
unique(lithics$Timeslice)
```

Figure 1 shows the time period and location distribution of the three types of lithics arranged on a map. The timeslices are arranged in 1000 year intervals between 15-11 ka BP. TS12 means timeslices 1-2 and TS13 means timesclices 1-3.This figure shows that geometric microliths spread the furthest out of all toolkits in TS4. The two TS3 points in spain of the geometric microlith graph shows that's where this tool kit was likely invented and then spread from there. It also shows that Zinken was most present in TS1, TS2, and TS3 but not in TS4. It also shows a pattern of movement to the West because older Zinken tools were found near Denmark and then more younger Zinken were found in the UK The Tanged points map shows that there were seen in both Denmark and up towards Latvia and then seen later in TS4 in between the two. This could suggest independent invention of Tanged points tool. To further analyze this dataset I can use ML to identify regions where toolkit traits shift over time using the length and weight columns. This might tell us wht the tool originated like and how it changes as it moves across space. This would help us answer the question if tanged points were individually invented. 

Predictions
My expected output will look like a FAMD factor map or a cluster plot. My benchmark will be a null model that randomly relabels the timescale for each point, 1,000 times. If my hypothesis is correct, the correlation in the benchmark model will be very low while the correlation in my model will be higher. If my null hypothesis is correct then both the benchmark and my analysis will have a low correlation. If my alternative explanation is correct then the benchmark and my analysis will show low correlation.
